title: Norse Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Old Norse pantheon mapped as a relationship graph: the giants and the making of the world from Ymir's body, the Aesir and the Vanir, the nine worlds on Yggdrasil, and the fixed road to Ragnarok.
sources: The Poetic Edda, translated by Henry Adams Bellows (1936)
Snorri Sturluson, The Prose Edda, translated by Arthur Gilchrist Brodeur (1916)
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, translated by Samuel Laing (1844)
The Volsunga Saga, translated by Eirikr Magnusson and William Morris (1888)
Saxo Grammaticus, The Danish History, translated by Oliver Elton (1894)
Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia for cross-checking manuscript attestation
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/norse/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

profile.cosmicNature: Linear, with a known ending. The world is built from the body of a murdered giant, runs its course, and is destroyed at Ragnarok in a battle whose participants and outcome are already fixed. A new green earth rises afterwards and a few survivors return, but the tradition puts almost all its weight on the ending rather than the renewal.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Mortal. The Aesir are stronger and longer-lived than men but they can be killed, they need Idunn's apples to stay young, and they know in detail how and by whom each of them will die. They are not creators of the moral order and are not omniscient; Odin spends the whole tradition trying to buy information he does not have, at increasing cost.
profile.afterlife: Divided by how you die rather than how you lived. Half the battle-slain go to Odin's Valhalla and half to Freyja's Folkvangr; the drowned go to Ran's hall under the sea; everyone else goes to Hel, which is not a punishment, merely dim. There is no judgment and no weighing - a bad man and a good man who die in bed arrive at the same place.
profile.systemMechanism: Fate outranks the gods. The Norns carve what will happen at the roots of the world tree, and neither Odin's knowledge nor Thor's strength alters it; Odin gathers warriors for a battle he knows he loses. What the tradition values is not escape but conduct - knowing the ending and going to meet it anyway, which is the nearest thing Norse religion has to a doctrine.
profile.canonTexts: The Poetic Edda, an anonymous collection of older verse; Snorri Sturluson's Prose Edda of about 1220; Heimskringla; the legendary and family sagas, above all the Volsunga Saga; and Saxo Grammaticus' Latin Gesta Danorum.

hierarchy.title: Before the World
hierarchy.blurb: Fire and ice meet across the yawning gap and the rime quickens into a giant. There is no creator here, only a first body and a cow who feeds it, and at the southern edge a fire-giant already waiting with a sword.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Odin and his brothers kill the giant and build the world from his body

hierarchy.title: The Aesir
hierarchy.blurb: The gods of Asgard are strong, quarrelsome and mortal. They stay young on Idunn's apples, they can be killed, and they know in detail how each of them will die.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: A war with the Vanir ends in an exchange of hostages

hierarchy.title: The Vanir
hierarchy.blurb: An older tribe of gods concerned with harvest, sea, wealth and magic rather than war and kingship. Njord, Freyr and Freyja come to Asgard as hostages of the truce and stay.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: The giants press from outside, and one of them lives inside the walls

hierarchy.title: The Giants
hierarchy.blurb: Older than the gods and not simply their enemies: the Aesir marry them, learn from them and depend on them. Loki is one, sworn brother to Odin and resident in Asgard.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Loki's three children are cast out, and each becomes exactly what was feared

hierarchy.title: The Brood and the Bound
hierarchy.blurb: Every measure taken against Loki's children is what makes the prophecy happen. The serpent thrown in the sea grows to circle the world; the wolf raised in Asgard and then betrayed kills Odin.
hierarchy.connectorCaption: Beneath all of it, three women at a well carve what will happen

hierarchy.title: Fate, and Those Who Meet It
hierarchy.blurb: The Norns outrank the gods, and neither Odin's knowledge nor Thor's strength alters a line of it. What the tradition values is not escape but conduct: knowing the ending and going to meet it.

stories.title: The Yawning Gap
stories.summary: In the beginning there is Ginnungagap, empty between the ice of Niflheim to the north and the fire of Muspelheim to the south, with Surtr already standing at the fire's edge with a flaming sword. Where the rime meets the warm air it drips and quickens into Ymir, the first living thing, who sleeps and sweats and begets from his own body. The cow Audhumla forms in the same melting and feeds him four rivers of milk, licking salty rime-blocks to feed herself. Over three days her licking uncovers a man in the ice - Buri, whose grandsons are Odin, Vili and Ve. So the gods and the giants both begin in the same thaw, from the same cow.

stories.title: The World Made from a Body
stories.summary: Odin and his brothers kill Ymir, and so much blood pours from him that every frost-giant drowns but two, who escape in a boat and father the rest. The three carry the corpse into the middle of Ginnungagap and build from it: the earth from his flesh, the mountains from his bones, boulders and scree from his teeth, the sea and lakes from his blood, the sky from his skull raised on four corners each held by a dwarf, and the clouds from his brains. Maggots in the flesh are given wits and become the dwarfs. The world is not made out of nothing and not made in goodwill: it is a body, taken apart by its own descendants.

stories.title: The Tree and What Eats It
stories.summary: Yggdrasil is an ash whose branches spread over every world and whose three roots reach to the Aesir, to the frost-giants and to Niflheim. Under one is Mimir's well of wisdom, under another the well of Urd where the Norns sit. It is under constant attack: a hart eats the shoots, four stags gnaw the branches, goats browse it, and Nidhogg chews the root from below, while the squirrel Ratatoskr runs the trunk carrying insults between the dragon and the eagle at the top. The Norns keep it alive by pouring white clay and well-water over it daily. Even the axis of the universe is a maintenance problem.

stories.title: The Eye at Mimir's Well
stories.summary: Wisdom and understanding are held in the well beneath one of the roots, and Mimir who keeps it drinks from it every morning. Odin comes and asks for a draught. Mimir names the price - an eye - and Odin pays it without recorded argument, and the eye lies in the well still. It is the first of the bargains that define him and the cheapest: he later hangs himself for the runes. What he buys is not power but information, and the tradition is precise that it does not save him. He knows exactly how Ragnarok goes, in detail, from this and other purchases, and it happens anyway.

stories.title: Odin on the Tree
stories.summary: Odin says it himself, in the first person: he hung on the windy tree nine full nights, wounded with a spear, given to Odin, himself to himself, on that tree of which no man knows from what roots it rises. No one gave him bread and no one gave him drink. He peered down, took up the runes screaming, and fell back. It is a self-sacrifice with no recipient but himself, and it buys the runes - writing, and the spells that go with them. The passage is one of the strangest in the corpus and has drawn endless comparison with the crucifixion, which the manuscript's Christian scribes may or may not have encouraged.

stories.title: The Mead of Poetry
stories.summary: The Aesir and Vanir seal their truce by spitting into a vat, and from the spittle they form Kvasir, who can answer anything. Two dwarfs murder him and brew his blood with honey into a mead that makes whoever drinks it a poet. They lose it to the giant Suttung as compensation for another killing, and he sets his daughter Gunnlod to guard it inside a mountain. Odin bores in as a snake, spends three nights with her, and drinks all three vessels; he escapes as an eagle with Suttung in pursuit, and spits the mead into containers in Asgard. A little spills on the way out, and that portion is the share of bad poets.

stories.title: The War and the Truce
stories.summary: The first war in the world is between the Aesir and the Vanir, and neither side wins. The sources are thin on causes - a witch called Gullveig burned three times and reborn, an exchange of insults, Odin casting a spear over a host - and clear on the ending: they trade hostages. Njord and his children Freyr and Freyja go to the Aesir; Hoenir and Mimir go to the Vanir. That arrangement half-fails, because the Vanir decide Hoenir is useless without Mimir prompting him, and behead Mimir and send the head back. Odin preserves it and consults it thereafter. The truce holds regardless, and the Vanir stay in Asgard permanently.

stories.title: The Builder and the Wall
stories.summary: A builder offers to wall Asgard in three seasons and asks for the sun, the moon and Freyja. On Loki's advice the gods accept, with one winter as the term, thinking it impossible - but the builder has a stallion, Svadilfari, who hauls stone all night at a rate that will finish the work early. Three days from the deadline the gods round on Loki and promise him a bad death. He turns into a mare, lures the stallion away into a wood, and the work stops. The builder loses his temper, reveals himself as a giant, and Thor kills him with the hammer despite the oaths sworn. Loki afterwards bears the eight-legged foal Sleipnir.

stories.title: The Forging of the Treasures
stories.summary: Loki cuts off Sif's hair for no stated reason, and Thor promises to break every bone in his body unless it is replaced. Loki goes to the sons of Ivaldi, who make hair of gold that grows, and also Odin's spear Gungnir and Freyr's folding ship Skidbladnir. Then he wagers his head that the dwarfs Brokkr and Eitri cannot match them. They make Odin's self-multiplying ring Draupnir, Freyr's golden boar, and Thor's hammer Mjollnir - short in the handle, because Loki as a fly bit Brokkr's eyelid and blood ran into his eye at the wrong moment. The gods judge the hammer the greatest. Loki forfeits, argues that he pledged his head and not his neck, and has his lips sewn shut instead.

stories.title: The Binding of Fenrir
stories.summary: Fenrir is raised in Asgard and only Tyr dares feed him. As he grows the gods decide to bind him and present two chains as tests of strength, both of which he breaks and enjoys. The third, Gleipnir, is made by dwarfs from the noise of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, a mountain's roots, a bear's sinews, a fish's breath and a bird's spittle, and is thin as a silk ribbon. Fenrir suspects a trick and agrees only if one of them puts a hand in his mouth as pledge. Tyr does, knowing what it costs. The fetter holds; the hand is bitten off; a sword is propped in the wolf's jaws to hold them open, and he lies bound until the end.

stories.title: The Theft of Idunn
stories.summary: Thjazi, in eagle shape, holds an ox off the fire until the travelling gods give him a share, then takes most of it; Loki strikes at him with a pole, is stuck fast, and is dragged until he agrees to deliver Idunn. He lures her out of Asgard with a story of better apples in a nearby wood, and Thjazi carries her off. Without her apples the gods begin to grey and stiffen within days. They work out who was last seen with her and give Loki the obvious choice. He borrows Freyja's falcon cloak, turns Idunn into a nut, and flies home with Thjazi in pursuit; the giant burns his wings on fires set along the walls and is killed inside them.

stories.title: Skadi Chooses a Husband by His Feet
stories.summary: Skadi comes to Asgard in mail with a drawn bow to avenge her father Thjazi. The gods offer settlement: she may choose a husband from among them, seeing only their feet, and they must make her laugh. She picks the finest pair, expecting Baldr, and gets Njord. Nobody can make her laugh until Loki ties a cord from his testicles to the beard of a goat, and the resulting tug-of-war ends with him falling screeching into her lap. She laughs, and Odin completes the settlement by throwing Thjazi's eyes into the sky as stars. The marriage then fails on geography: nine nights in her mountains, nine at his shore, and each cannot bear the other's home.

stories.title: Thor in a Wedding Dress
stories.summary: Thor wakes to find Mjollnir gone. Loki, in Freyja's falcon cloak, finds Thrym on a mound plaiting collars for his hounds and entirely pleased: the hammer is eight leagues underground and the price is Freyja. Her refusal is violent enough to shake the halls and snap her necklace. Heimdall proposes dressing Thor as the bride instead. Thor objects that the gods will call him unmanly; Loki observes that giants will otherwise be living in Asgard by evening. Veiled, Thor eats an ox, eight salmon and three casks of mead, and Loki explains each alarming detail as bridal excitement. When the hammer is laid in the bride's lap to hallow the marriage, Thor takes it and kills every giant in the hall.

stories.title: Thor Fishes for the World Serpent
stories.summary: Thor goes with the giant Hymir to fetch a cauldron big enough to brew ale for the gods, and they row out to fish. Thor takes the head of Hymir's best ox for bait and insists on rowing far past the giant's usual grounds. He hooks Jormungandr. The serpent thrashes, Thor braces so hard his feet go through the hull to the sea floor, and he hauls it up until the two are face to face, the serpent spitting venom - and as Thor reaches for his hammer, Hymir cuts the line in terror. The serpent sinks back. The scene appears on carved stones from England to Sweden, which suggests it was one of the best known stories in the north.

stories.title: The Journey to Utgard
stories.summary: Thor and Loki shelter overnight in what proves at dawn to be the thumb of a giant's glove. At Utgard the king sets them contests and they lose every one: Loki is out-eaten, their servant out-run, Thor cannot drain a horn, cannot lift a grey cat past one paw, and is forced to one knee by an old woman. Leaving, humiliated, they are told the truth - Loki raced wildfire, the runner raced thought, the horn's far end was in the sea and Thor lowered it visibly, the cat was the world serpent and he lifted it until the sky was touched, and the old woman was old age, who has never been thrown by anyone. Then the castle vanishes.

stories.title: The Duel with Hrungnir
stories.summary: Odin wagers his head that no horse in Jotunheim can match Sleipnir, and Hrungnir's Gullfaxi keeps up so closely that the giant rides straight through the gates of Asgard. Given hospitality he drinks Thor's cups and announces that he will sink Asgard, kill the gods and take Freyja and Sif home. Thor arrives and a formal duel is arranged. The giants build a clay man nine leagues tall to second him and put a mare's heart in it, so it is terrified before anything starts. Hrungnir throws his whetstone and Thor throws Mjollnir; they meet in the air, the hone shatters and a fragment lodges in Thor's head, and the hammer kills the giant, whose falling leg pins Thor to the ground.

stories.title: The Wooing of Gerdr
stories.summary: Freyr sits in Odin's high seat, which he should not, and sees a woman whose arms light the air and the sea. He goes home sick and will not speak. His servant Skirnir gets the story out of him and agrees to go, taking Freyr's self-fighting sword as payment. Gerdr refuses apples of gold and the ring Draupnir flatly. Skirnir then threatens her with a rune-carved curse: madness, a monstrous husband, endless desire never satisfied, and life among the frost-giants where she will be jeered at. She yields, and agrees to meet Freyr in nine nights. The bargain costs Freyr his weapon, and at Ragnarok he faces Surtr without it and dies.

stories.title: The Oaths Taken from Everything
stories.summary: Baldr dreams of his own death and tells the Aesir. Odin rides down to a seeress's grave and wakes her to ask; she tells him the hall is prepared for Baldr's coming. Frigg takes a different approach and goes round the whole world exacting an oath from every thing that it will not harm him - fire, water, iron, every metal, stones, earth, trees, sicknesses, beasts, birds, poisons and serpents. It works completely. The gods amuse themselves at the assembly by throwing weapons at Baldr and watching them refuse to bite. Loki, disguised as a woman, asks Frigg whether anything was left out, and she says only a young mistletoe west of Valhalla, too small to bother with.

stories.title: The Death of Baldr
stories.summary: Loki makes a dart of the mistletoe and finds Hodr standing outside the ring of throwers because he is blind and has nothing to throw. He offers to direct him. The dart goes through Baldr and he falls dead, and the gods stand speechless, unable to take vengeance because the assembly ground is sanctuary. The body is carried to the ship Hringhorni; Nanna's heart breaks at the sight and she is laid on the pyre beside him. Thor hallows the fire with his hammer and kicks a passing dwarf into it. Odin lays Draupnir on the pyre and whispers something in his son's ear that no one hears, and which no source ever reveals.

stories.title: Hermod's Ride to Hel
stories.summary: Frigg asks who will ride to Hel and offer a ransom, and Hermod goes on Sleipnir. He rides nine nights through valleys so dark he sees nothing, reaches the gold-roofed bridge over Gjoll, and is told by its guardian that he does not have the colour of a dead man. He jumps the gate outright. Baldr is sitting in the seat of honour. Hel agrees to release him if every thing in the world, living and dead, weeps for him - and everything does, except one giantess in a cave who says she will weep dry tears and that Hel may keep what she has. She is generally taken to be Loki. Baldr stays.

stories.title: The Flyting at Aegir's Hall
stories.summary: Aegir gives a feast and Loki, having killed a servant, forces his way back in on the strength of his blood-brotherhood with Odin. He then insults every god present in turn, and the accusations are specific and mostly sexual: Bragi is brave on his bench, Idunn embraced her brother's killer, Freyja has had every god and elf in the hall, Njord's own sister bore his children, Tyr has one hand, Odin practised the unmanly seidr and gave victory to cowards, Frigg took his brothers to bed. Nobody successfully answers him. Only Thor's arrival, and the direct threat of the hammer, drives him out, and Loki leaves promising that Aegir will never hold such a feast again.

stories.title: The Binding of Loki
stories.summary: Loki hides in a house on a mountain with four doors, and by day becomes a salmon in the waterfall. Sitting by the fire he plaits the first fishing net out of linen, and burns it when the gods approach - but Kvasir reads the ash. They net the river; Loki leaps the first cast and is caught in the second when Thor grabs him mid-air by the tail, which is why salmon taper. The gods turn one of his sons into a wolf that tears the other apart, and bind Loki to three stones with those entrails, which harden to iron. Skadi fixes a serpent above his face to drip venom. Sigyn stays with a bowl, and when she turns to empty it the earth shakes.

stories.title: Gefjon Ploughs Zealand
stories.summary: King Gylfi of Sweden offers Gefjon as much land as she can plough in a day and a night. She goes to Jotunheim, bears four sons to a giant, turns them into oxen, and yokes them to a plough that bites so deep it tears the land loose and drags it west into the sea, where it becomes Zealand. The hole left behind fills with water and becomes lake Malaren, and Snorri notes that the bays of the lake match the headlands of the island. He quotes a verse by the ninth-century poet Bragi as his evidence, which by his standards is unusually good attestation, and repeats the story in Heimskringla as history rather than myth.

stories.title: Valhalla and the Einherjar
stories.summary: Half the battle-slain go to Odin's Valhalla and half to Freyja's Folkvangr, and the sources say Freyja chooses first. Valhalla has five hundred and forty doors, each wide enough for eight hundred men abreast, and a roof of shields. The einherjar fight each other all day, are killed and healed and rise again, and feast all night on the boar Saehrimnir, which is boiled every day and whole again by evening, washed down with mead from the goat Heidrun. Bragi greets them as they arrive. The entire arrangement is a standing army being assembled for a battle Odin already knows he loses, which the dead are not told.

stories.title: Ragnarok
stories.summary: Three winters without summer, brothers killing brothers, the wolf swallowing the sun. Garmr howls before Gnipahellir, the fetters break and Fenrir runs free. The serpent thrashes ashore, Loki steers a ship of the dead from Hel, Surtr rides out of Muspell and Bifrost breaks under the host. Heimdall blows Gjallarhorn and the einherjar march out. Odin is swallowed by Fenrir and Vidar tears the wolf apart; Thor kills Jormungandr and walks nine paces before the venom drops him; Freyr, weaponless, falls to Surtr; Tyr and Garmr kill each other; Loki and Heimdall kill each other. Then Surtr flings fire over everything and the earth sinks into the sea.

stories.title: The Green Earth After
stories.summary: The earth rises a second time out of the sea, green, and eagles fish in the falls. Vidar and Vali live, and Thor's sons Modi and Magni inherit Mjollnir. Baldr comes back from Hel with Hodr and they sit together in the grass and talk over what happened, and find the gold gaming pieces of the old gods lying in the meadow. Two humans, Lif and Lifthrasir, survive by hiding in a wood and repopulate the world. A hall roofed with gold stands at Gimle for the good. And then, in the last stanza, Nidhogg flies over carrying corpses in his wings, and the seeress sinks - which is either a fragment out of place or the bleakest ending in European literature.

stories.title: The Otter's Ransom
stories.summary: Odin, Loki and Hoenir kill an otter by a waterfall and take its skin, and stop for the night with Hreidmar, who recognises it as his son Otr and demands the skin be stuffed and covered with gold. Loki borrows Ran's net, catches the dwarf Andvari in the shape of a pike, and takes his whole hoard including the ring Andvaranaut, which the dwarf tries to keep back. As Andvari goes he curses the ring and every piece of the gold to destroy whoever owns it. One whisker is left showing on the skin and the ring covers it. Then Fafnir and Regin kill their father for the gold, and the curse begins its work.

stories.title: Sigurd and Fafnir
stories.summary: Regin fosters Sigurd and works on him to kill Fafnir. He forges swords that Sigurd snaps on the anvil until Sigurd brings the fragments of his father's sword Gram, reforged from those, which splits the anvil and cuts a tuft of wool floating downstream. Regin advises digging a pit in the dragon's track to the water and stabbing upward. Sigurd does, and Fafnir dying speaks with him at length, warning that the gold is cursed and will kill him too. Regin then asks him to roast the heart. Sigurd burns his thumb, sucks it, and instantly understands the birds overhead, who are discussing Regin's plan to kill him. He beheads Regin and takes the gold.

stories.title: The Wall of Flame
stories.summary: Riding on, Sigurd sees a light on a mountain and finds a wall of flame around a sleeping figure in mail so tight he must cut it off with his sword. It is Brynhildr, a valkyrie whom Odin pricked with a sleep-thorn and shut behind fire for awarding victory to the wrong king. She teaches him runes and wisdom and they swear themselves to each other. Then he rides to the Gjukungs, whose queen gives him a drink that erases her from his memory entirely, and he marries Gudrun. Worse, he later takes Gunnar's shape to ride the flames a second time and win Brynhildr for him, and she marries Gunnar believing it was his doing.

stories.title: The Quarrel at the River
stories.summary: Brynhildr and Gudrun quarrel while washing in the river over whose husband is the greater and who may stand upstream of whom. Gudrun ends it by producing the ring Sigurd took from Brynhildr on the night he rode the flames in Gunnar's shape. Brynhildr now knows she was deceived into the wrong marriage by the only man she ever swore to. She does not weep. She goes to Gunnar and tells him Sigurd broke faith with him, and keeps at it until Sigurd is murdered - in his bed in one version, in the forest in another. Then she laughs once aloud, gives away her gold, stabs herself, and asks to be laid on his pyre with a drawn sword between them.
